pr.title: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code (REQ-2297)
pr.body:
Requirement: REQ-2297

Agent-written implementation of requirement REQ-2297 (upstream MessagePack-CSharp issue 2297), from the Junction 2026 challenge branch `ju26-issue-2297`.

Author: coding agent. Accountable owner: to be assigned by Countersign.
pr.author: ToukoUrsin

requirement.title: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.
requirement.body:
#### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.
MessagePack generated code is not decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.

Because it is very hard to write good coverage for generated MessagePack code, it may skew coverage numbers, especially on large projects with a lot of generated code.

#### Describe the solution you'd like
I would like all generated code to be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.  I do not feel like a setting is needed, but setting would be fine to have too.

#### Describe alternatives you've considered
There are no alternatives, it is close to impossible to write good coverage for generated code as it covers many edge cases.

#### Additional context

N/A

story.headline: Formatter, resolver and helper classes produced by the MessagePack source generator now carry [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage], so coverage tools skip them, except when the consuming project targets netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework.
story.before: Generated formatter and resolver classes had no ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute. Coverage tools counted them as uncovered code, which lowered coverage numbers in projects with many MessagePack types.
story.after: Every generated enum, int-key, string-key and union formatter, the resolver class, and its FormatterCache<T> and GetFormatterHelper nested classes are emitted with [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] inside `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. In builds where either symbol is defined, the attribute is not emitted.

steps.text: The four formatter templates (enum, int-key object, string-key object, union) and their pre-generated .cs files write the guarded attribute above each formatter class.
The resolver and composite-resolver templates add the same guarded attribute to the partial resolver class and to its nested FormatterCache<T> and <Name>GetFormatterHelper classes.
EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces now writes a newline after the opening brace of a constrained enclosing type. Without it, the `#if` line would land on the same line as the brace and fail to compile.

A new CodeCoverageExclusionTests class runs the generator on a mixed sample and checks that each generated file contains the attribute and that every occurrence sits inside the `#if` guard. 221 snapshot files are updated to match the new output.
The README states that generated formatters and resolvers carry the attribute, except on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework.

alsoTouches: The attribute is placed on the user-declared partial resolver class, so it applies to members the user writes in their own part of that class.
Projects targeting netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework get no attribute, because of the preprocessor guard.
Generated code for constrained nested generic types now has a line break after the enclosing type's opening brace, which changes the snapshot for F85.
The composite-resolver generator (CompositeResolverGenerator) emits the attribute on its resolver output as well, not only the main MessagePackGenerator.

findings.title: Guard strips the attribute for netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework consumers, where it exists
findings.body: Every emitted attribute is wrapped in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. The code comment and README say the attribute is unavailable on those targets, but `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` is part of .NET Framework 4.0+ and .NET Standard 2.0, and is valid on classes there. So any SDK project targeting net472/net48 or netstandard2.0 gets no exclusion at all, which fails AC1/AC3 for those targets; MessagePack itself ships for exactly those targets (src/MessagePack/MessagePack.csproj:4). I did not compile a netstandard2.0 consumer to confirm availability; this rests on the BCL API surface.
findings.scenario: A net472 or netstandard2.0 library with [MessagePackObject] types uses the generator. The SDK defines NETFRAMEWORK / NETSTANDARD2_0, the `#if` block is skipped, no generated formatter or resolver carries the attribute, and coverage numbers are still skewed by generated code.

findings.body: The generator now puts `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` on its part of the resolver partial class, both for `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver]` and `[CompositeResolver]` types. Those classes are declared by the user, and the attribute does not allow multiple instances, so a user who already put it on their own part gets a duplicate-attribute compile error (CS0579) after upgrading. That is exactly the workaround a user affected by this issue would have applied. I did not compile this case; no snapshot or test covers a resolver whose user part already carries the attribute.

After this change the generated part adds a second ExcludeFromCodeCoverage, and the build fails with CS0579 where it compiled before.
findings.suggestion: Skip the attribute on the resolver partial when the user's declaration already has it (check the symbol's attributes in the generator), or do not attribute the user-owned partial at all and attribute only the generated members and nested types. Add a test with a pre-attributed resolver.

findings.title: Generated namespace-container partial classes are emitted without the attribute
findings.body: For data types in a namespace, the generator emits intermediate container classes such as `internal partial class MyTestNamespace` inside the resolver, and these do not get the attribute. They hold no executable code and sit inside the attributed resolver, so the coverage effect is probably nil on targets where the resolver is attributed. Read literally, AC1 ("every type ... and any helper types") is not met for them.

findings.suggestion: Either accept this explicitly (the containers have no code) or state it in the README; attributing them here is not straightforward because the same code path also emits user-owned nesting types.

discarded.title: Attribute on user-extendable partial resolver: CS0579 duplicate and user code excluded
discarded.claimed: The resolver and composite-resolver templates put ExcludeFromCodeCoverage on the generated half of a `partial class` whose other half is written by the user (the PR's own test declares `partial class GeneratedMessagePackResolver`). The attribute is AllowMultiple=false, so a user who already has it on their half gets a CS0579 duplicate-attribute compile error after upgrading. An attribute on one partial declaration applies to the whole type, so hand-written members the user adds to their resolver

discarded.claimed: Every emitted attribute is wrapped in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`, and the README says the attribute is unavailable on those targets. To my knowledge System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute ships in .NET Framework 4.0+ and in netstandard2.0, and is valid on classes there. Consumers on net472/net48 or netstandard2.0 therefore get no exclusion at all, which fails AC1, AC2 and AC3 for those supported targets. The README statement that justifies it looks factually
discarded.detail: Same defect as "Guard strips the attribute for netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework consumers, where it exists" (raised by the correctness lens); merged.

discarded.title: New tests check one attribute per file, not one per generated type
discarded.claimed: `AllGeneratedTypesAreExcludedFromCodeCoverage` only asserts that each generated file contains the attribute string at least once. The resolver file declares three types (the resolver, FormatterCache<T>, the GetFormatterHelper), so the test still passes if two of them lose the attribute. The second test only compares the attribute count with the guarded count, which holds for any count above zero. No test covers the CompositeResolver generator, and none parses with NETSTANDARD2_0 or NETFRAMEWORK
discarded.detail: Same defect as "New tests check one attribute per file, not per type, and never exercise the guard" (raised by the correctness lens); merged.

refusals.question: Should the attribute be emitted for netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework consumers, or is excluding those targets intended?
refusals.why: The requirement leaves handling of older frameworks open. The choice decides which users get the feature and what compile risk the project accepts on older or unusual targets (e.g. Unity profiles), which is a compatibility-policy call.

options.label: Keep the guard (no attribute on netstandard2.0 / .NET Framework)
options.consequence: Consumers on net472/net48/netstandard2.0 get no coverage exclusion; README statement that the attribute is unavailable there stays, although the BCL does define it on those targets.

options.label: Emit unconditionally
options.consequence: All SDK targets get the attribute; generated code fails to compile only on a target that truly lacks the type, which nobody in this review has enumerated.

refusals.context: ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute is in .NET Framework 4.0+ and .NET Standard 2.0. The MessagePack library itself targets netstandard2.0, netstandard2.1, net8.0 and net472. Unity does not define NETSTANDARD2_0 or NETFRAMEWORK, so Unity projects get the attribute regardless of API profile under the current guard.

refusals.question: Should the attribute be applied to the user-extendable partial resolver class itself, which also excludes any hand-written members in that class, or only to purely generated nested types and members?
refusals.why: This is a product-intent choice between the simplest reading of 'all generated code' and not silently changing coverage or compilation for user-written code in the same partial type. The requirement leaves this open.

options.label: Attribute on the outer partial resolver class
options.consequence: The whole resolver, including user-written members, is excluded from coverage. Users who already have the attribute on their half get CS0579.

options.label: Attribute only on generated nested types and generated members
options.consequence: No effect on user code and no duplicate-attribute risk. It needs member-level attributes on GetFormatter and similar members in the resolver.

refusals.context: The resolver classes are declared `partial` by the user and extended by the generator. The PR's test source declares `partial class GeneratedMessagePackResolver` in user code.
